It is uncertain to me whether the *author* wrote a *preface* to this *treatise* or not; and I could wish that the small spark of living desire for *true knowledge* within me were able to write anything worthy of an *introduction* to this *book*. This work is a *true mystical mirror of the highest wisdom*; for although I have been educated in the *schools of learning* and have made some progress in *languages* and the *arts* according to my limited ability, yet I acknowledge myself to be but an unlearned *beginner* <note>original: "A. B. C. Scholler"</note> in *Wisdom’s* <note>original: "Sophia's"</note> *school*, who would gladly learn to read her *first lessons* <term>original: "Christs Cross line"; the first line of an alphabet in a child's primer, often preceded by a cross</term>.

Indeed, the best *treasure* that a person can attain in this *world* is *true knowledge*—even the *knowledge* of oneself. For *man* is the great *mystery of God*, the *microcosm* <term>a miniature representation of the whole universe</term>, or the complete *summary of the whole universe*. He is the *marvelous work of God* <note>original: "Mirandum dei opus"</note>, *God’s masterpiece*, a *living symbol* and *sacred representation* <term>original: "Hierogliphick"</term> *of eternity and time*. Therefore, to know where he comes from and what his temporal and *eternal being*—and *well-being*—is, must surely be that *one necessary thing* at which all our chief *study* should aim. In comparison to this, all the *wealth of this world* is but *loss* and *rubbish*.

Hence *Solomon*, the *wisest* of the *kings of Israel*, says: "Happy is the man who finds *wisdom*, and the man who gets *understanding*. For the *merchandise* of it is better than the *merchandise* of *silver*, and the gain from it better than fine *gold*. She is more *precious* than *rubies*, and all things that can be desired are not to be compared to her," etc.

This is that *wisdom* which dwells in *nothing* and yet possesses *all things*, and the *humble, yielded soul* is

If you ask, "*What is the way to attain this Wisdom?*" Behold! Christ, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life, tells you plainly in these words (Luke 9:23): *If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his Cross daily, and follow me*; or as He says elsewhere, *Unless you are born again, you cannot see the Kingdom of Heaven*; or as St. Paul says, 1 Cor. 3:18, *If any man seems to be wise in this world, let him become a fool, that he may be wise.*

Herein lies that simple, childlike way to the highest *Wisdom*, which no sharp *Reason* or worldly learning can reach; indeed, it is foolishness to *Reason*, and therefore so few go the way to find it. The proud *Sophisters* <term>deceptive or superficial reasoners</term> and *wiselings* <term>those who think themselves wise in worldly matters but lack true spiritual insight</term> of this world have always trampled it underfoot with scorn and contempt and have called it *Enthusiasm* <note>In the 17th century, "enthusiasm" was a derogatory term used to mock those claiming to have direct, personal divine inspiration</note>, *madness*, *melancholy*, *whimsey*, *fancy*, etc. But *wisdom is justified of her children*.

Indeed, everyone is not fit for, or capable of, the knowledge of the *Eternal* and *Temporal Nature* in its *Mysterious operation*; neither is the *proud, covetous world* worthy to receive a clear manifestation of it. Therefore, the *only wise God (who gives Wisdom to everyone who asks it rightly of Him)* has locked up the Jewel in His

For the *Mysteries* of *Philosophy*, *Divinity*, and *Theosophy* must not be profaned or laid open to the view of outward *Astral Reason* <term>intellect influenced only by the physical world and celestial alignments, lacking spiritual insight</term>, which turns everything toward its selfish *Pride*, *Covetousness*, *Envy*, *Wrath*, and *cunning Hypocrisy*. They are like the cloudy *Pillar* of *Moses*: they have a dark part and a light part. They are dark to the *Egyptians* (the *Pharisaical Sons* of *Sophistry* <term>deceptive or superficial reasoning</term>), but light to the true *Israel*, the children of the *Mystery*.

# The Preface to the Reader.

Then his Eternal Spirit may enter into that which is "within the veil" <note>A biblical reference to the inner sanctuary of the Temple, symbolizing direct access to the presence of God</note> and see not only the literal, but the *moral*, *allegorical*, and *anagogical* <term>mystical or spiritual interpretation</term> meaning of the *wise* and their dark sayings. 

He then, I say, will be fit to enter not only into *Solomon’s Porch* <note>The outer portico of the Jewish Temple; here representing the beginning of natural knowledge</note>, the outer court of natural philosophy, sense, and reason, but likewise into the inward court of holy and spiritual exercises in divine understanding and knowledge. And so he may step into the most inward and holiest place of *Theosophical Mysteries* <term>divine wisdom or mystical knowledge of God</term>, where no one is admitted to come except those who have received the high and holy *Unction* <term>anointing or spiritual blessing</term>.

But lest I should overstep by being too long-winded, I will endeavor briefly to hint to the reader what this book contains, even though the spirit of *Wisdom* within it cannot be described with pen and ink any more than a sound can be painted, or the wind grasped in the hollow of the hand. But know that here, the author vividly <note>original: "lively"</note> deciphers and represents to you the *Signature of All Things* <term>the spiritual idea that every physical thing bears a mark or sign of its inner essence</term>, and gives you the contents of *Eternity* and *Time*, and glances at all *mysteries*.

In this book, the author fundamentally sets forth the birth, sympathy, and antipathy of all beings: how all beings originally arise out of one *Eternal Mystery*, and how that same Mystery begets itself within itself from eternity to eternity. Likewise, he shows how all things that take their origin out of this *Eternal Mystery* may be changed into evil, and then back from evil into good, with a clear and manifest demonstration of how man has turned himself out of the good and into the evil, and how his *transmutation* <term>the changing of one substance or state into another, often used in alchemy</term> is again out of the evil and into the good. Moreover, it declares here the outward cure of the body: how the outward life may be freed from sickness by its likeness or assim- <meta>catchword: -ilation</meta>

# The Preface to the Reader.

...and speaking of God's *Works* and *Wonders* in the dispensation of his *Wisdom*; then your doubtful, unsettled *Jupiter* <note>In the astrological language used by Boehme, Jupiter represents the soul’s desire for justice and wisdom, which is "unsettled" until transformed by God</note> will be turned into a *Plerophory* <note>original: "Plerophory" — from the Greek 'plerophoria', meaning full conviction or absolute certainty</note>, or a most full assurance of true joy and saving comfort in your religion; your earthly *Venus* <note>Representing earthly desire or lust</note> into heavenly *Love*, and your eclipsed, mutable *Luna* <note>The moon, representing the changing and unstable nature of the human mind</note> into the pure, perfect, and crystalline streams of *Light, Life*, and *Glory*.

But the proud *scorner* who will take no warning belongs to *Lucifer’s regiment* <note>Lucifer's army or followers</note>. He saw that the *Mystery* of God’s kingdom consists of *meekness, simplicity*, and deep *humility*; therefore, out of his pride, he aspired to be above the divine *Love* and the *harmony* of obedience to God’s *will*. Thus, he fell into the *Abyss* of the dark *world*, even into the outermost darkness of the first Principle, which we call Hell, where he and his legions are captives. May the Almighty God of Love deliver us from this. Amen.

And so I will end with the words of the *Author* <note>Jacob Boehme</note> at the conclusion of the *book*, where he says this:

> I have faithfully, with all true admonition, represented to the reader what the Lord of all beings has given me; he may behold himself in this looking-glass, within and without, and so he shall find what and who he is. Every reader, whether he be good or bad, will find profit and benefit in it. It is a very clear gate to the Great Mystery of all beings. Through glosses, comments, curiosity, and self-wit <note>Personal cleverness or intellectual pride</note>, no one shall be able to reach or understand it in its own ground; but it may very well meet and embrace the true seeker, and create much profit and joy for him—yes, be helpful to him in all natural things—provided that he applies himself to it rightly and seeks in the fear of God. For it is still a time of seeking, as a lily blossoms <note>The "blossoming lily" is Boehme's famous metaphor for a coming spiritual renewal or the blooming of the divine life within the soul</note> upon the mountains and valleys in all the ends of the earth: He who seeks, finds.

And so I commend the reader to the grace and love of *Jesus Christ*, in whom are hidden all the *treasures* of *wisdom* and *knowledge*.

->Yours in the true service of all Christian love,<-
->J. ELLISTONE.<-

<meta>This page begins the first chapter of Jacob Boehme's "The Signature of All Things." It follows the translator's preface, which established the spiritual necessity of moving from earthly desires to divine certainty. Here, Boehme begins his core argument: that all true knowledge of God and nature requires understanding the "Signature"—the internal character or "likeness" that God has imprinted on all created things.</meta>

# The Signature of All Things, J. B. <note>Jacob Boehme</note>

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>* The Being of all Beings <note>original: "Ens Entium"</note>.</margin>
*How everything that is spoken of God without the knowledge of the **Signature** is mute and lacks understanding; and that in the mind of man, the **Signature** lies very accurately composed according to the **Essence of all Essences**.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring floral motifs and symmetrical scrollwork.</image-desc>

1. Everything that is spoken, written, or taught about God without the knowledge of the **Signature** is mute and void of understanding. It proceeds only from a historical conjecture, repeated from the mouth of another, in which the spirit is silent because it lacks knowledge. But if the Spirit opens the **Signature** to a person, then he understands the speech of another. Furthermore, he understands how the Spirit has manifested and revealed itself (out of the **Essence** through the **Principle**) in the sound of the voice. Just because I see someone speaking, teaching, preaching, and writing about God—and even if I hear and read it myself—it is not enough for me to understand him. But if his sound and spirit, coming out of his **Signature** and **likeness** <note>original: "Similitude"</note>, enters into my own likeness and imprints his likeness into mine, then I may understand him truly and fundamentally—whether it is spoken or written—provided he has the hammer that can strike my bell.

2. By this we know that all human properties proceed from One; they all have only one Root and Mother. Otherwise, one person could not understand another through sound. For through sound or speech, the **Form** marks and imprints itself into the likeness of another. One similar tone or sound catches and moves another; and in that sound, the Spirit imprints its own likeness, which it conceived in the **Essence** and brought to form in the **Principle**.

3. So that in the word it may be understood where the Spirit

<sig>B</sig>
<meta>catchword: has</meta>

<summary>Boehme introduces the "Signature," an internal blueprint or "likeness" in all things that allows for true communication and understanding of God. He argues that without personal spiritual insight into these Signatures, religious teaching is merely empty repetition.</summary>
<keywords>Signature, Essence, Principle, Similitude, spiritual communication, Jacob Boehme, inner knowledge</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening chapter of Jacob Boehme's "The Signature of All Things." It concludes the previous sentence's thought that one person's internal character or "Signature" can influence and resonate with another's, much like musical instruments tuning to one another.</meta>

# The Signature of All Things. CHAPTER I.

<margin>* Or, formed itself; or, originally brought itself forth.</margin>
...has \* conceived, whether for good or evil. With this **Signature**, he enters into another person's form and awakens a similar form within that person’s **Signature**. In this way, both forms harmonize into one, creating a single comprehension, one will, one spirit, and also one understanding.

4. Secondly, we must understand that the **Signature** or **Form** is not the Spirit itself, but rather the **receptacle, container**, or **cabinet** of the Spirit where it resides. The **Signature** exists within the **Essence** <note>original: "Essence"; here meaning the underlying substance or "being" of a thing.</note> and is like a **lute** that remains still. It is a silent object that is neither heard nor understood on its own; but if it is played upon, then its **Form** is understood—revealing its tuning and the notes to which it is set. Likewise, the **Signature of Nature** is a silent **Essence** in its natural form; it is like a prepared musical instrument upon which the **Will-spirit** plays. Whichever strings he touches will sound according to their specific properties.

<margin>* Proceeds from the mouth. * Or, conception.</margin>
5. In the human mind, the **Signature** lies most skillfully <note>original: "artificially"; in the 17th century, this meant "with great art or skill."</note> composed according to the **Essence of all Essences**. Man lacks only the wise Master who can strike his instrument—which is the true Spirit of the high Power of Eternity. If that Spirit is quickened in a person, stirring and acting in the center of the mind, then it plays upon the instrument of the human form. It is only then that the form is \* expressed <note>original: "uttered"</note> through the sound of the word. The instrument sounds according to how it was tuned at the time of his \* **incarnation**, and his knowledge follows suit. The inner self reveals itself through the sound of the word, for that is the mind's natural knowledge of itself.

6. Man indeed possesses the forms of all three Worlds <note>In Boehme’s mystical philosophy, the "three worlds" are the dark world of God’s fire/wrath, the light world of God’s love, and the external, visible world.</note> within him; for he is a complete image of God, or of the Being of all beings. However, the specific order of these forms is established within him at his **incarnation**. There are three "Work-masters" in him who prepare his **Form** [or **Signature**]: namely, the threefold **Let it be done** <note>original: "Fiat"; the Latin command used by God in Genesis to create the world.</note> according to the three Worlds. These masters compete for control over the Form, and the Form is shaped according to this **contest**. Whichever of the Masters holds the dominant rule and gains control over the **Essence**, the instrument is tuned to him. The other masters remain hidden and their sounds stay in the background, as is clearly visible in life.

7. As soon as a person is born into this world, his spirit begins to play upon his instrument. His innate, genuine **Form** [or **Signature**]—whether for good or evil—is seen through his words and **conduct** <note>original: "Conversation"; in this period, it referred to one's entire manner of living, not just speech.</note>. Just as his instrument sounds, so do his senses and thoughts emerge from the essence of his mind. Thus, the **external spirit of the will** is reflected in his behavior. This can be seen in both humans and animals, where there is a great difference in how each is produced—that one...

He explains that a person's character and knowledge are determined by which of the "three worlds" dominates their internal "tuning" during their formation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Chapter 1 of Jacob Boehme's "The Signature of All Things," further exploring how the internal character (the "Signature") of a person or object can be influenced, changed, and recognized through outward signs.</meta>

# CHAPTER I. The Signature of All Things <note>original: "Signatura Rerum"</note>.

Brother and sister do not act the same as each other.

8. Furthermore, we should know that although one *Creative Word* <note>original: "Fiat"; the Latin command "let it be done," referring here to the formative power of nature.</note> maintains control and shapes the form according to itself, the other two qualities still produce their own sound if their instrument is played upon. This is seen in how many people—and even animals—though strongly inclined toward either good or evil, can be moved toward the opposite by a *Counter-tune* <note>original: "Contra-tune"</note>. They often let their inbred *Signature* [or *Figure*] fall away when this *Counter-tune* is played upon their hidden *Lute* or *Form*. We see that a wicked person is often moved to repent and stop their iniquity by a good person, when the good person touches and plays upon the wicked person's hidden instrument with their own meek and loving spirit.

9. This also happens to a good person: when a wicked person strikes the good person’s hidden instrument with a spirit of wrath, the form of anger is awakened in the good person too. One is set against the other so that one might become the *Cure* and *Healer* of the other. For just as the *Vital Signature*—that is, the form of life—is shaped during the *Creative Word* <note>original: "Fiat"</note> at the time of *Conception*, so is its natural spirit; it arises out of the *Essence* of all three *Principles* <note>Boehme refers to his theological system of three "worlds": the dark fire-world, the light world, and the external world of nature.</note> and manifests its actions and will according to those properties.

10. However, the will can be broken. When a stronger force arrives and awakens the inner *Signature* with its own introduced sound and spirit of will, the dominant quality loses its power, right, and authority. We see this in the powerful influence of the *Sun*: by its strength, it modifies <note>original: "qualifieth"</note> a bitter and sour fruit, turning it into something sweet and pleasant. Similarly, a good person can be corrupted in bad company, and a good herb cannot fully show its true, natural virtue in poor soil. In the good person, the hidden instrument of evil is awakened; in the herb, a contrary *Essence* is absorbed from the earth. In this way, good is often changed into evil, and evil into good.

<margin>* His appearance or facial features <note>original: "Physiognomy"</note>.</margin>
11. And now look! As the power and dominance of a *Quality* <note>original: "Quality"; here meaning an internal property or character.</note> stands within, so it is signed and marked externally in its outward *Form, Signature,* or *Figure*. In humans, this is shown in speech, will, and behavior, as well as in the shape of the body parts used for that *Signature*. A person's inward form is noted in the *form* of their face. This is also true for animals, herbs, and trees: everything is signed outwardly exactly as it is inwardly (in its innate virtue and quality). And even if it happens that a thing changes from evil to good or good to evil, it still keeps an external *Character* so that the change <note>the shift from the original state to the new one</note> may be recognized.

12. For a person is known in this regard by their daily habits, as well as by their thoughts and actions; for the "upper instrument" <note>Boehme uses the metaphor of a musical instrument to describe the human soul or psyche.</note>, which is most strongly drawn, is always the one being played. It is the same with a wild beast: even when it is overawed and tamed, and brought to a different temperament, it does not easily show its original, innate form—unless it is provoked. Then, that original nature breaks out and appears above all other forms.

13. It is the same with the plants of the Earth. If a plant is transplanted from poor soil into good soil, it soon gains a stronger body and a more pleasant scent and power, showing its inner Essence outwardly. There is nothing created or born in Nature that does not also manifest its internal form externally, for the internal continually labors or works itself toward manifestation. We recognize this in the power and form of this world: how the one and only Essence has manifested itself through an "External Birth" <note>The physical creation or material manifestation of spiritual reality.</note> into the physical world as a Reflection <note>original: "Similitude"</note>; and how it has manifested itself in so many forms and shapes, which we see and recognize in the stars and elements, as well as in living creatures, trees, and herbs.

<margin>* In</margin>

14. Therefore, the greatest understanding is found in the "Signature," through which a human being (namely, the image of the Greatest Power <note>original: "Vertue"</note>) may learn to know not only themselves, but also the "Essence of all Essences." For by the external form of all creatures—by their impulses, inclinations, and desires, as well as by the sounds, voices, and speech they utter—the hidden Spirit is known. Nature has given a language to everything according to its essence and form; for the language or sound arises out of the Essence, and the Creative Word <note>original: "Fiat"; the divine command "let it be done."</note> of that Essence forms the quality of the nature into the voice or power it sends forth: it gives sound to the animals and gives scent, power, and form to the *Essentials* <note>The underlying spiritual qualities of physical things.</note>.

15. Everything has its own "mouth" for manifestation. This is the language of Nature, through which everything speaks from its own properties and continually manifests, declares, and sets itself forth according to what it is good or useful for. Each thing manifests its "Mother" <note>In Boehme’s philosophy, the "Mother" refers to the source, origin, or the specific "mould" of nature from which a thing is born.</note>, which provides the Essence and the Will to the Form.

<header>CHAPTER 2. The Signature of All Things <note>original: "Signatura Rerum"</note></header>

## CHAPTER II.

### *Of the Opposition and Combat in the Essence of all Essences, by which the Basis of Antipathy and Sympathy in Nature may be seen, as well as the Corruption and Cure of each thing.*

1. Since there are so many and diverse forms, where each one continually produces and provides out of its own property a will different from others, we understand from this the opposition and combat in the Being of all Beings. We see how one thing opposes, poisons, and kills another—that is, it overpowers the other's essence and the spirit of that essence, forcing it into another form. This is the origin of sickness and pain: when one essence destroys another.

2. And from this, we understand the cure: how one thing heals another and restores it to health. If this did not exist, there would be no Nature, only an eternal stillness and no Will. For it is the "counter-will" <note>original: "Contra-will"; the concept that life and motion require friction or opposing forces to exist.</note> that creates motion and the origin of the "Seeking." The opposing sound seeks rest, yet in that seeking, it only elevates and further ignites itself.

<margin>* Made sick.</margin>
3. We are to understand how the cure of each thing consists in the "similitude" <term>original: "Assimulate"; refers to a substance of a similar nature or "likeness"</term>; for in the similar substance, the Will finds its satisfaction, namely, its highest joy. Each thing desires a will of its own likeness, and it is made sick <note>original: "discomfited"</note> by the counter-will. But if it obtains a will of its own likeness, it rejoices in that similar substance and falls into rest, and the enmity is turned into joy.

4. For Eternal Nature has produced nothing in its desire except a likeness of itself. If there were not a perpetual mixing, there would be an eternal peace in Nature; but then Nature would not be revealed or made manifest. It is through combat that Nature becomes manifest, so that each thing elevates itself and tries to escape the combat into "still rest." In doing so, it runs to and fro, and by that very motion, it only awakens and stirs up the combat further.

5. We find clearly in the "light of nature" <note>The innate wisdom or divine understanding present within the created world.</note> that there is no better help or remedy for this opposition, and no higher cure, than Liberty—which is the light of nature and the desire of the Spirit.

6. And then we find that the essence cannot be better remedied than

...than with its like <term>original: "Assimulate"; refers to a substance of a similar nature or "likeness"</term>; for the Essence is a Being, and its desire is for Being. 7. Since we see that human life consists of three Principles—namely, in a threefold Essence—and also has a threefold Spirit arising from the property of each Essence: first, according to eternal Nature (the property of fire); second, according to the property of eternal Light and divine Essentiality; and third, according to the property of the outward world. Therefore, we must consider the property of this threefold Spirit, and also of this threefold Essence and Will. We must see how each Spirit, along with its Essence, brings itself into strife and sickness, and what its cure and remedy is.

8. We understand that apart from Nature there is an eternal stillness and rest—namely, the "Nothing." We then understand that an eternal Will arises in that Nothing to bring the Nothing into "Something," so that the Will might find, feel, and behold itself.

9. For in the Nothing, the Will would not be manifest to itself. Therefore, we know that the Will seeks itself and finds itself within itself. Its seeking is a desire, and its finding is the essence of that desire, in which the Will finds itself.

<margin><image-desc>A faint hand-drawn manicule (pointing hand) in the left margin pointing towards paragraph 10.</image-desc></margin>
10. It finds nothing except the property of hunger, which is itself, and which it draws into itself. That is, it draws itself into itself and finds itself within itself. Its attraction into itself creates an overshadowing or darkness within it, which does not exist in the "Liberty"—that is, in the Nothing. For the Will of the Liberty <term>original: "Liberty"; here referring to the unconditioned, free state of the divine "Nothing" before creation</term> overshadows itself with the essence of the desire; for it is the desire that creates the essence, and not the will.

11. Now, the fact that the Will must be in darkness is its opposition <note>original: "Contrariety"</note>. It conceives within itself another Will to go out from the darkness and back into the Liberty—namely, into the Nothing. And yet, it cannot reach the Liberty from outside of itself, for the desire goes outward and causes a source <note>original: "source"; often used by Boehme to mean a "quality," "sting," or "painful welling up" of motion</note> and darkness. Therefore, the Will (meaning the "re-conceived Will") must enter inward, and yet there is no separation.

12. For within itself, before the desire, is the Liberty—namely, the Nothing. And the Will cannot simply be a "Nothing," for it desires to manifest itself in the Nothing. Yet no manifestation can be achieved except through the essence of the desire. And the more the re-conceived Will desires manifestation, the more

This happens in a two-fold form: according to the Delightful Will of the Liberty in a source of Joy, and according to the Delightful Will of the anxious desire. According to the contracting force <note>original: "Astringency"</note>, it is stinging <note>original: "Compunctive"</note>, bitter, and envious from the sting; and according to the anguish of the Wheel, it is wholly murderous and hateful. Each property dwells in itself, and yet they are in one another. In this, God’s Love and Anger are understood: they dwell in each other, and the one does not seize the other, yet one is the Curer of the other. 12. The desire draws into itself strongly and eagerly, creating three Forms within itself. These are: the Desire, which is astringent <note>original: "astringent"; a contracting or shrinking force</note> and creates hardness because it is an enclosing force, from which coldness arises; and the attraction, which causes a stinging <note>original: "Compunction"</note> and a stirring within that hardness—a conflict <note>original: "enmity"</note> against the very hardness it attracted. This attraction is the second Form and the cause of motion and life. It stirs within the contraction and hardness, but the hardness (the enclosure) cannot tolerate this stirring. Therefore, it pulls even more eagerly to contain the stinging motion, yet the stinging only becomes stronger because of it.

13. Thus, the stinging "compunction" strives to move upward and whirls crosswise, yet it cannot achieve its goal because the hardness (the desire) stops and detains it. Therefore, it stands like a triangle and a reversed orb. Since it cannot move from its place, it begins to wheel or rotate. This creates a mixture within the desire—the "essence" or the many-sided nature of the desire. This turning causes a continual confusion and grinding <note>original: "Contrition"</note>, from which "Anguish"—the third Form (the sting of the senses)—arises.

14. It exists in a hard, stinging, dry essence and cannot escape or rid itself of it; for the will itself creates the essence and also possesses it. In this way, the will finds itself emerging from the "Nothing" into the "Something." Yet this "Something" is still contrary to its original will, for it is a state of unrest, while the free will is a state of stillness.

15. This is the origin of conflict <note>original: "Enmity"</note>: that Nature opposes the free will, and a thing is at odds within itself. Here we understand the "Center of Nature" with its three Forms. In the beginning (in the first Principle), it is "Spirit"; in the second, it is "Love"; and in the third Principle, it is "Essence." In this third Principle, these three Forms are called *Sulphur*, *Mercury*, and *Salt* <note>original: "Sal"</note>.

16. Understand it in this way: *Sul* is, in the first Principle, the free will or the "inclination" <term>original: "Lubet"; from the German "Lust" or "Liebe," meaning a longing, delight, or divine inclination</term> to move from "Nothing" to "Something"; it exists in liberty, apart from Nature. *Phur* is the desire of that free inclination, which creates an "Essence" within itself. This essence is harsh <note>original: "Austere"</note> because of the attraction and develops itself into three Forms (as mentioned above), and eventually into the fourth Form: "Fire." In the word *Phur*, the origin of both eternal and external Nature is understood; for hardness is the "mother" and the preserver of the intensity <note>original: "sharpness"</note> of all essences.

Understand "Essence" in relation to Agitation <note>original: "Perturbation"; referring to the internal stirrings or disturbance that precedes creation</note>; for the "Nothing" is silent and without motion, but this Agitation makes the Nothing active. However, in the third Principle—namely, in the governance of the Essence and the source of the physical world—this Form is called Mercury <term>Mercury: in Boehme's thought, the active, restless, and often chaotic life-force that causes motion, sensation, and the "working" of nature</term>. It is conflicting, harsh, and poisonous, yet it is the cause of life and movement, as well as the cause of the senses. In this state, a single thought or spark of the will <margin>A thought or spark of the will</margin> can perceive itself within infinity and then immerse itself into it, whereby the unsearchable and infinite variety of the universe arises out of the One.

22. This Form represents restlessness, yet it seeks rest; and in its seeking, it causes further restlessness. It makes itself its own enemy. Its cure is twofold because its desire is twofold: first, according to the Delight <term>original: "Lubet"; the free, divine inclination or "willing" toward goodness, peace, and the "liberty" of the Nothing</term> of liberty, which involves stillness and meekness; and second, in the hunger that arises from restlessness and the discovery of itself. The Root desires only joy through the primary Will, yet it cannot obtain it except through its opposite source. No joy can arise in the silent "Nothing"; it must arise only through motion and rising <note>original: "Elevation"</note> so that the Nothing may find itself.

23. Now, that which has been found desires to return to the will of the Still Nothing, so that it may have peace and rest within it. The "Nothing" is its cure, while the wrath and "poison" (the harsh, active qualities) serve as the remedy for the one who seeks and finds. This is the life they discover. We see an example of this in the bitter gall <note>original: "poysonful gall"; referring to bile or the bitter principle in the body, which Boehme relates to the spark of life</note>, from which both joy and sorrow arise in life. In this, we also understand a twofold will: one toward the wrathful fire and anxious, painful life at the origin of nature; and the other toward the light-life—the joy of nature—which has its origin in the eternal Nothing.

24. The cure for the first will is the Delight <note>original: "Lubet"</note> of Liberty. If it attains this, it creates a triumphant joy within itself. Meanwhile, the wrath within the hungry desire acts as the healer and helper of the other will—the will of Nature. Through this, God's love and anger are understood, as well as how evil and good exist within the center <margin>In the center</margin> of every life. It shows how no joy could arise without sorrow, and how one serves as the healer of the other.

25. Here we understand the third will (which originates from both of these—that is, from such an essence, or from the "mother"), which is the Spirit. The Spirit contains both of these properties; it is both a product <note>original: "son"</note> of these properties and their master. In the Spirit lies the power; it may awaken whichever property it pleases. The properties lie within the essence and are like a well-structured life, or like a musical instrument with many strings <margin>Or, voices</margin> that remain silent until played. The Spirit—that is, the Outgoing <term>original: "Egresse"; the movement of the spirit outward from the internal essence into manifestation</term>—is the real Life that may play upon them.

...the instrument as he pleases; in evil, or good; according to love or anger. As he plays, and as the instrument sounds, so is it received by its counter-tenor, namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, by that which is similar to it.

26. If the tune of Love is played—namely, the desire of Freedom <note>original: "Liberties desire"</note>—then the sound is received by that same Freedom and "Love-Lubet" <term>Lubet: a term used by Boehme for a longing, delight, or divine inclination</term>. If the instrument is struck according to the desire of Nature—namely, in wrath, anger, and bitter falsehood—then the same counter-sound and wrathful desire receives it. This is because it matches its own nature and satisfies its hunger. In this, we understand the desire of both the light world and the dark world; a dual source and nature.

<margin>* Or, God.</margin>
28. The desire of Freedom is meek, easy, and pleasant, and it is called Good <note>original: "* Good"</note>. The desire of Nature makes itself dark, dry, hungry, and wrathful within itself, which is called God’s anger and the dark world—namely, the first Principle. The light world is the second Principle.

29. We must understand that these are not divided essences. Rather, one holds the other hidden or closed up within it. One is the beginning and cause of the other, and also its healing and cure. Whichever is awakened and stirred up gains mastery; it manifests itself externally with its own character and creates a form and "Signature" <term>Signature: the outward physical mark or appearance that reveals an object's inner spiritual essence</term> according to its will in the external world. We see a likeness of this in an enraged man or beast; although the outward man and beast are not in the inward world, the <margin>* Nature. * World.</margin> outward nature possesses the very same forms. This is because nature arises originally from the inward world and stands upon an inward root.

30. The third Form is Anguish <note>original: "Anxiousnefs"</note>, which arises in Nature from the first and second Forms. It is the sustainer or preserver of the first and second. Within itself, it is the sharp "Let it be" <note>original: "Fiat"; the divine command of creation</note>. The second Form possesses the "Word" <note>original: "Verbum"</note>—the property of expression. It consists of three properties, and out of itself, it makes a fourth with those three: namely, Fire. In the external birth—namely, in the third Principle—this is called Salt <note>original: "Sal"</note>, according to its physical matter. But in its spirit, it has many forms, for it is the root of fire and the "Great Anguish." It arises between and out of the harshness <note>original: "Astringency"</note> and bitterness in the stern contraction. It is the essence of that which is attracted—namely, the physical body or tangibility. From Sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur"</note>, it is sulfurous, and from Mercury <note>original: "Mercury"</note>, it is a blaze or flash. In itself, it is painful—namely, a sharpness like dying—and that comes from the sharp attraction of the harshness. It has a two-fold fire...

...one cold, another hot. The cold arises from the Astringency <term>Astringency: the quality of drawing together or contracting; the first form of nature</term>—from the sharp attraction—and is a dark, black fire. The hot arises from the driving compunction <margin>Or, the sting of instigation.</margin> within the anguish of the desire for Freedom; and Freedom is its enkindler, and the raging compunction <margin>* Raiser, enkindler, or inflamer.</margin> is the awakener of the cold fire.

31. These three forms are in one another as one, and yet they are but one; but they separate themselves through their origin into many forms. Yet they have but one Mother—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, the desiring Will toward manifestation, which is called the Father of Nature and of the Being of all beings.

32. Now we are to consider the hunger of the anxiety, or the Salt-spirit <term>Salt-spirit: in Böhme’s alchemy, the principle of stability and physical substance formed by contraction</term>, and then also its satiating or fulfillment. From the origin of the first Will (which comes out of Freedom for the purpose of self-manifestation), the anguish has two wills within it. The first will is directed toward Nature. The other, re-conceived will is the "Son" of the first, which goes out of manifestation again and back into itself, into Freedom. It has become an Eternal Life in Nature, and yet it does not possess Nature essentially; rather, it dwells in itself and penetrates Nature like a transparent shine. The first will goes outward <margin>* Or, out of itself.</margin>, for it is the desire for manifestation; it seeks itself outside of itself, and yet gathers the desire within itself. It desires to bring forth <note>original: "educe"</note> the internal out of itself.

33. Thus it has two properties. With the seeking within itself, it creates the Center of Nature; for it is like a poison, a will of dreadful ambition, like a lightning strike and thunder-clap. This desire only wants anguish and to be terrible, so that it may find itself within itself—coming out of the "Nothing" and into the "Something." The second form proceeds forth as a "flagrat" <term>Flagrat: a sudden flash, stroke, or explosion of sound or light</term>, or a produced sound out of itself. It is not the desire of the first will to remain in a state of horrible death, but only to bring itself out of the "Nothing" in this way and to find itself.

34. By the Center within itself—with its ambitious wrathfulness and the wrathful will toward Nature—we understand the dark world. By the movement <note>original: "egress"</note> out of itself toward manifestation, we understand the outward world. And by the second will (which comes out of the first and enters again into Freedom), we understand the light world, the Kingdom of Joy, or the true Godhead <note>original: "Deity"</note>.

35. The desire of the dark world is for manifestation—namely, for the outward world—to attract and draw that same substance <note>original: "essentiality"</note> into itself, and thereby satisfy its wrathful hunger. The desire of the outward world is for the Essence or Life which arises from pain and anguish.

36. Its desire within itself is the Wonder of Eternity, a mystery, or a mirror, or that which is grasped by the first will toward Nature.

### Chapter 2. The Signature of All Things <note>original: "Signatura Rerum"</note>. 12

37. The outward world's desire is for *Sulphur, Mercury*, and *Salt* <note>original: Latin terms for the "Tria Prima," the three primary substances of alchemy</note>; for it is such an essence in itself—namely, a hunger after itself—and it is also its own satisfaction. For *Sul* <note>Boehme identifies *Sul* with the light or the Sun</note> desires *Phur* <note>Boehme identifies *Phur* with the fire</note>, and *Phur* desires *Mercury*, and both of these desire *Salt* <note>original: "Sal"</note>. For *Salt* is their solace <note>original text partially hidden: "Sol-"; likely "Solace"</note> which they hatch in their desire, and which afterward becomes their habitation and also their food.

38. Each desire only wants the essentiality of *Salt* according to its own property; for *Salt* is diverse. One part is the sharpness of cold, and one part is the sharpness of heat; also one part is brimstone <term>Brimstone: sulfur, associated with fire and the soul</term> and one part is saltpeter <note>original: "Salniter"</note> from *Mercury*.

39. These properties exist within one another as one, but they separate <note>original: "seve-"</note> themselves, each dwelling in itself; for they are of a different essence. When one enters into another, there is enmity and a flash-stroke <term>Flagrat: a Latinate term used by Boehme to describe a sudden, violent eruption or ignition, like a lightning strike or a chemical reaction</term>. We may understand a likeness of this in thunder and lightning. This happens when the great anguish—namely, the "Mother of all Salts" (the third form of Nature)—compresses itself. This occurs due to the influence of the Sun, which stirs up the form of the hot fire so that it becomes penetrative, as is the property of fire. When it reaches the saltpeter, it ignites itself. The saltpeter is in itself the great flash-stroke within *Mercury*—namely, the flash or the stinging motion <note>original: "compunction"</note> which enters into the coldness, as well as into the cold sharpness of the salt-spirit. This coldness is exceedingly terrified by the flash of the fire and, in an instant, wraps or folds itself up within itself. From this arises the thunder-clap (or the tempestuous flash, which delivers a strike during the flash-stroke). The flash-stroke goes downwards because it is heavy due to the coldness; however, the saltpeter-spirit is light due to the fire, and this spirit carries the thunder or sound sideways, as is heard in tempests and thunder. Immediately afterward, the wind or spirit comes out from all four forms against one another, for all four are ignited in the penetrating flash-stroke. Whereupon hail and rain follow. The hail folds itself together in the coldness, in the property of the cold salt-spirit; for the "Wrath" <note>the harsh, contracting quality of nature</note> attracts it to itself and turns the water to ice. The water arises from the "meekness"—namely, from the desire for the Light—for water is the physical substance of meekness. This the cold salt-spirit congeals into drops and distills upon the Earth; for before this congealing, it is only like a mist, steam, vapor, or dampness.

40. Thus we see this ground very exactly and properly in thunder and lightning; for the flash, lightning, or ethereal blaze always goes first, for it is the ignited saltpeter. Thereupon follows the strike in the flash-stroke of the coldness. As you see, as soon as the strike is given, the "astringent chamber" <note>the contracted or enclosed state of the elements</note> is opened...

## CHAPTER III.

->Of the Grand Mystery <note>original: *Mysterium Magnum*</note> of all Beings.<-

1. Courteous reader, observe the meaning correctly. We do not mean by this description a "beginning" of the Deity, but we show you the manifestation of the Deity through Nature. For God is without beginning, and has an eternal beginning and an eternal end, which he is himself. The nature of the inward world has been in the same essence from eternity.

<margin>Mystery</margin>
2. We give you this to understand regarding the divine essence: without Nature, God is a mystery <note>original: *Mysterium*</note>. Understand that this is in the "Nothing," for outside of Nature is the "Nothing," which is an eye of eternity—an abyssal <term>Abyssal: relating to the *Ungrund*, the "bottomless" or "unfounded" state of God before creation</term> eye that stands or sees in the "Nothing," for it is the abyss. This same eye is a Will—understand it as a longing for manifestation, to find the "Nothing." But now there is nothing before the Will where it might find something, or where it might have a place to rest; therefore, it enters into itself and finds itself through Nature.

<margin>Similitude, Likeness, or Signature</margin>
3. And we understand in the mystery without Nature two first forms: one directed toward Nature—toward the manifestation of the "Wonder-Eye"—and the second form is produced out of the first, which is a desire for virtue and power, and is the first Will’s son, its desire for joyfulness. Understand us thus: the desire flows out <note>original: "is Egressive"</note>, and this outflowing is the spirit of the Will and desire, for it is a moving. This desire makes a form <note>original: *Signatura*</note> in the spirit, namely, the forming of the infiniteness of the mystery.

4. And this form (or likeness) is the eternal wisdom of the Deity. We understand herein the Trinity of the only Deity, whose ground we must not seek to know—specifically, how the first Will arises in the abyss from eternity, which is called "Father." We only know the eternal birth and distinguish the Deity—namely, what purely and merely concerns the Deity, or the Good, from Nature—and show you the secret <note>original: *Arcanum*</note> of the greatest secret mystery: namely, how the abyss, or the Deity, manifests itself with this eternal...

Understand, then, that in the first Desire (which arises in the longing for liberty), all things exist and are made substantial and essential. This is how the creation of this world proceeded; we find within it the properties of the Earth, as well as all metals, stones, and also the *stars* <note>original: "Astrum"</note> and the origin of the elements—all coming from one single mother, which is the "Lubet" and the Desire from which all things proceeded and still proceed.

13. For *Mercury* is generated within Sulphur; it is the "Severing"—that is, the separation of light and darkness from one another. It is the "breaking wheel" and the cause of various divisions or multiplicity. It separates the dark essentiality from the essentiality of light—namely, the metals from the gross, restrictive, dark, stony, and earthly property. The property of the Desire gives and creates dark essence, and the property of the free "Lubet" creates light essence—namely, metals and everything of a similar kind and appearance.

<margin>* In.</margin>

For the Desire attracts very forcefully to itself, and this attraction creates the motion or "sting of trembling" (or a terrifying remorse), and that which is compressed is the anguish. But if liberty is included within it, liberty rejects it, and there arises the origin of enmity and the "Severing," so that one form separates from another and a two-fold will arises.

Now, if the wrath enters so forcefully into itself that it raises the saltpeter-flash, it then seizes the substance of the free Longing within itself, from which the flash arises. For there, the wrath seizes the meekness, which is just as if water were poured into fire, creating a sudden explosion <note>original: "Flagrat"</note>. Then the wrath of the great anguish dies, and joy ascends with the flash. The flash comes out of *Mercury*, or out of the anguish of death, and also becomes material; but because of the Liberty, it changes itself into white, which is Saltpeter. Now, if the fire—the horrible, anxious sharpness—enters it again, the saltpeter is startled and gives a clash <note>original: "Repulse"</note>; for the first property (which existed before the "death") is ignited again with the sulfurous spirit. You can see a clear example of these properties in gunpowder.

21. Secondly, a salt-water is generated from the astringent, harsh, and attractive drawing-in property; its matter is Salt. For there is as much diversity of sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone"</note> and salt as there is variety of taste and fire to be found in all creatures, herbs, and trees. Also, everything that lives and grows has sulfur and salt; for the salty property attracts and preserves the * body, and * the sulfur has within it the oil or light in which the free longing toward manifestation consists, from which growth arises.

## CHAPTER 3.

22. Thirdly, there is brought forth through the salt-nitral flash <note>original: "Salnitral Flagrat," an alchemical term for a sudden, explosive burst of energy or saltpeter</note> out of the property of the bitter, stinging <note>original: "compunctive"</note> attraction—in the first impression in the Spirit—an earthly property of water. Its matter <note>original: "Materia"</note> is Earth; for this arises from the dark essentiality where the darkness impresses itself in the first Desire (in which the darkness arises, as was mentioned before). Thus, out of its property in that impression, it begets a mist, smoky steam, or vapor, which the flash in the salt-nitre seizes. Its essence is then dismayed or "dies," and falls downward. This is the matter of the Earth; although the Earth is not of only one sort, it contains everything that became physical <note>original: "Corporeal"</note> in the flash—all of which springs through the "death" of the Earth, according to how it was wrapped and driven together into a lump during Creation, as we plainly see.

23. Further, we are to consider the highest secret <note>original: "Arcanum"</note>: namely, the heavenly essentiality, and then the precious stones and metals. We must consider where they all take their rise and origin, seeing as all things come out of one Mother, which is the longing <note>original: "Lubet"</note> and desire of Eternity for its own manifestation.

24. Now, concerning the incorruptible essence of physicality <note>original: "Corporality"</note>, it also arises in the first desire for Nature. Yet it arises in the impression of the free longing <note>original: "Lubet"</note> and goes along through all the forms even into the highest sharpness, where it retires again into itself, like a life out of the Fire. The Eternal Fire is magical, and a Spirit, and does not die; Liberty is its igniter, but the eternal Nature is its sharpness. This same essence loses the property of "wrath" in the Light. In that fire, it is like a dying—yet there is no dying, but rather an entrance into another source: namely, out of a painful desire into a love-desire. It also yields Spirit and essence from the Fire-spirit, and the essence of meekness from the Light.

<margin>* Gives, yields, or affords.</margin>

25. For that which "dies" to the Fire, or sinks through death, is divine essence. This is likewise effected through the salt-nitral flash of divine joyfulness, where the property trembles in the joy of meekness and immerses itself through the death of the Fire (which is called God’s Anger) and quenches it, so that God dwells in a meek Light. # Signatura Rerum. CHAP. 3. <note>original: "The Signature of All Things"</note>

Death or the *Flash* <note>original: "Flagrat," Boehme’s term for the sudden, energetic ignition where spirit becomes matter</note> falls down into the *Divine Freedom* <note>original: "Liberty"</note> as something powerless and freely surrenders itself. Then the *Spirit*—that is, the *Source* (meaning the very sharp, fiery, and anxious *Source* of life)—becomes material and retains only an essential way of working, like a powerless desire. In the igniting of the fire within the *Saltpeter-like Flash* <note>original: "Salnitral Flagrat," referring to a spiritual chemical reaction like the explosion of gunpowder</note>, each *Property* separates within itself, and the entire *Matter* <note>original: "Materia"</note> is divided into specific parts: namely, into metals, stones, and earth.

<margin>* Or, the highest or most noble metals.</margin>

However, because the *Freedom* is also contained there along with the property of *Sulphur* <note>original: "Sul"</note> or *Light*, the *Sulphur* pushes outward to manifest itself, as is the nature of *Freedom* to do. Thus, that very flash or glimmer also becomes material in the *Flash*; therefore, they are hard and have a blinking glance like an *Eye*. <margin>* Liquid.</margin>

If man could open (or reveal) the dead body of the metal and reduce it to a * *flying, moving Spirit*—which can only be accomplished through *Divine Motion*—then it would be seen what it could become; no *Reason* believes or understands this without divine *Vision*.

Sixthly, the Venusian <note>original: "Venerine"</note> man, according to the outward desire and the property of water. Seventhly, the Solar man, according to the Sun’s property—that is, according to the outward world—as a seer and knower of the wonders of God. And yet, he is but one single man; he exists both in the inward and outward world. This is likewise the likeness of the seven metals: having one property according to the inward world, and another visible, tangible property according to the outward world.

35. From Jupiter, the sphere turns round, and out of the separation Mercury proceeds forth with a "broken" metal, according to his spirit’s property. # CHAPTER 4. The Signature of All Things <note>original: "Signatura Rerum"</note>

...and speeches. It is written, *God has made all things by His Word.* The heavenly, eternal Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> is His Word, which the Father expresses in the kindling of His light; that which is expressed is His Wisdom. The Word is the worker, framer, and maker of the forms within that expressed Wisdom. Now, what the inward Mercury does internally within God’s power, the outward Mercury likewise effects in the outward power of the created essence. For he carries the fire-spirit in sulfur into all the planets, forming and giving to each thing its source and true spirit of life.

37. Mars, in the first impression, is the great anguish. This causes the "love-will" of liberty to separate from him; and that which is severed is called God. The anguish, or fire-source, is called God’s anger—namely, the wrath of the eternal nature. Just as God’s love internally separates from God’s anger—that is, from the wrathful property of eternal nature, separating heaven from hell and God from the Devil—so also is this effect produced in the birth of the outward nature.

38. Love proceeds out of the wrath and is an act of humility or submission. In this way, it also came into order during the Creation. Therefore, Venus stands in the sphere on the line of Mars, under the Sun, for such is the separation in nature; thus one proceeds forth from another. Its metal is copper. The origin of this is that love is a desire, and it desires only light and joy, for matter <note>original: "Materia"</note> is made out of the desire of property. But if the love-desire is to become corporeal <note>to take on a physical body</note> in the impression, then it must resign itself to the wrathful creative command <note>original: "Fiat," Latin for "let it be done"</note>—namely, to the desire of Mars in the fire, or in the fiery property. For the Saturnine property takes everything into its power and makes it corporeal.

## CHAPTER V.
### *Of the Sulfurous Death, and how the dead Body is revived, and replaced into its first Glory.*

1. All life and motion, along with understanding, reason, and senses, both in animals and plants, consist originally in **Sulfur**—namely, in Nature's Desire, and in the **Lubet's** desire of the liberty <term>the Lubet: Boehme's term for the "Divine Pleasure" or the free, spontaneous inclination of the spirit toward manifestation</term>.

2. In Nature's desire arises death and enclosure, and in the desire of the liberty arises the opening and the life. For the desire of liberty transforms the desire of the dark nature, so that the wrathful Mother lets go of her own right and freely resigns to the desire of liberty; and so, life grows in death, for there is no life without light. But if the light goes out in the essence of the **Sulfur**, then it is an eternal death, which no man can revive, unless God moves Himself in the **Lubet-desire** within that same death; for death itself can receive no life.

<summary>Boehme describes the Sun as the central transforming power that turns the "wrathful" planetary forces of Saturn and Mars into growth and joy. He introduces the concept of the "Lubet," the divine inclination that brings life and light out of the restrictive enclosure of death.</summary>

## CHAPTER VI.

### *How Water and Oil are generated, and of the difference between Water and Oil, and of Vegetable Life and Growth.*

<margin>* Of, or belonging to Nature.</margin>
1. All Life, Growth, and stimulation consist in two things, namely: in the **Lubet** <note>original: "Lubet." From the German *Lust*, meaning a subtle, passive inclination, delight, or "free will" that exists before active desire begins.</note> and in the **Desire**. The Lubet is a free will and is like a "nothing" in comparison to Nature; but the Desire is like a hunger. In the Desire arises the moving spirit—that is, the natural spirit—and in the Lubet arises the supernatural spirit, which yet belongs to nature, not out of its own property, but out of [or from] the property of the Desire.

<margin>† Being, Matter, or Food.</margin>
2. The Desire is the stimulation of the **Essence** <note>original: "Essence." In this context, it refers to the fundamental substance or "being" of a thing.</note> (namely, a hunger), and the Lubet is the hunger’s † essence [or food], which it takes into itself. For the Desire is only a hungry will, and it is the natural spirit in its forms; but the Lubet is out of the **Liberty** <note>original: "Liberty." Boehme uses this to describe the "Unground" or the state of God's being before or beyond the constraints of nature and desire.</note>. For God is desire-less concerning his own essence, insofar as he is called God; for he needs nothing, All is his, and he himself is All.

3. But he has a Lubet-will, and he himself is the Will to manifest himself in the Lubet. Yet in the free, affection-less Lubet, no manifestation can be achieved because it is void of Desire. It is as if it were nothing in respect to Nature, and yet it is All. But this is not according to Desire (that is, according to Nature), but according to the satisfying of Nature; it is the satisfying of the hungry Desire (namely, of Nature). It freely and willingly gives itself into the hunger of Nature; for it is a Spirit without essence and desire, wholly free as a "nothing." But the Desire **essentializes** <note>original: "essentialize [or materiate]." To turn a spiritual impulse into a physical or substantial reality.</note> it within itself, and that according to two properties: one according to the Eternal Liberty, which is free from the **Source** <note>original: "Source." Often used by Boehme to refer to the *Qual*, the painful or active "working" of nature.</note>; and the other according to the Desire, which gives a vegetative life (namely, a growing, or a giving forth of itself).

4. The Free Essence is and gives an **Oil** <note>original: "Oyl." Here representing a spiritual substance or fuel that allows for the light of life to shine.</note>, and the property of Desire gives a life to the Oil. The Oil is a Light, and the property of Desire gives the Essence to the Light (namely, the fiery property), so that the Light shines, as is seen in fire and light. And the free Lubet remains a free will in itself, but gives its meekness (namely, a free resignation) into the Desire, so that it...

There is also no other possibility within it, for it is as a "Nothing," in which no disturbance or source of agitation can exist; rather, it is meekness itself.

5. But because it cannot remain a "Nothing"—since it is a cause and beginning of the **Desire** <note>In Boehme’s system, Desire is the contractive, hungry force that creates matter out of spirit.</note>—it gives itself freely, just as sunshine freely gives itself to every property. The Desire conceives [or takes] this free **Lubet** <note>original: "Lubet." To the same degree that property exists in the Desire, there is also an equal degree of essence. 6. But seeing that the Desire (which is the hunger) is filled with the free Lubet, it also turns its own property into essence within the essence of the Liberty. Its essence is Water, and the essence of the free Lubet is an Oil. Thus, a two-fold property arises in one single spirit: namely, a fiery property according to the property of the Desire, and a joyful or luminous property according to the Liberty.

In the outward world, this is called a **Fire**, but in the property of the inward worlds, where the Desire acts within the property of the free Lubet, this desire is called the **divine Desire**. In this desire, the fiery Love burns and joyfulness arises. The free Lubet gives itself into the harsh Desire so that it may bring forth a fiery Love—that is, a joyfulness—which could not exist in the still Lubet; for where there is stillness, there is no joy or motion.

Nothing, and this is now the "Seeing" <note>Boehme refers to the divine vision or awareness emerging from the void.</note>.

13. For when the **brilliance of the fire** <note>original: "Fire-splendor."</note> tastes the sweetness of the Light, then the fire’s desire reaches after the gentleness <note>original: "Meekness." As we see, as soon as the Light shines, it strips the Darkness of its power; therefore, God is a Lord over all beings, for He is the eternal power and light. A likeness of this can be seen in the sun, which is lord over the darkness and all substances, ruling whatever grows, lives, and moves in this world.

14. Furthermore, we are to consider the various **Salts**, how they arise in the Origin and separate into many properties. In the Origin of the **compression** <note>original: "Impression." The other Salt is the sharpness of the compression, according to the quality of the contracting harshness; this is the anguish within the compression, which is **Sulfur** <note>original: "Brimstone."</note>, and its basic quality is water.

15. The water is the lifeless, mortal quality of the Salt; and the sulfurous quality, which comes from the anguish, is the quality of the "living" salt. For it contains the sting of motion—namely, the **Mercury** <note>In the Paracelsian tradition used by Boehme, Mercury represents the principle of movement, communication, and life-force.</note>—which creates the form of life. And yet, sulfur is not the salt itself, but rather the anguish within the compression, which also becomes physical.

16. The salt is the sharpness within the sulfur regarding its contraction; the salt causes the anguish to become **physical** <note>original: "Corporeal."</note>. Thus, salt lives within the sulfur and is its sharpness, preserving the sulfur in its physical substance, as well as the spirit of the sulfur, so that it does not fall to dust. The salt compresses the powers of the anguish, and the compressed life is the "Mercurial" life; this is the life of the anguish (that is, of the sulfur), and it divides the **matter** <note>original: "Materia."</note> according to the forms of nature. It also divides the matter of the free inclination into two substances: a watery one and an oily one, and finally into a physical form.

17. This physical form is twofold, appearing in both the Darkness and the Light. According to the property of the harsh Desire, it creates a sandy or stony nature within the watery element—this is the origin of stones, coming out of the sulfurous water (the water of the sulfur).

It also divides the matter of the free Lubet into two substances: first into a watery and oily state, and then into a physical body.

According to the property of the harsh Desire, it creates a sandy or stony nature within the watery property; this is the origin of stones, which come out of the Sulfurous quality—that is, out of the "Sulfur-water."

The <term>sulfurous</term> <note>original: "Sulphrous."</note> part, which comes from the anguish, is the property of the "living" salt, for it contains the "sting of motion"—that is, the <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercury." In alchemy, mercury represents the principle of fluidity, transformation, and the "spirit" of life.</note>—within it, which forms the shape of life. And yet the sulfur is not the salt itself, but rather the anguish within the compression, which also becomes physical.

16. The salt is the sharpness within the sulfur, relating to its harshness. The salt causes the anguish to become physical; thus, salt dwells in the sulfur and is the sulfur’s sharpness. It preserves the sulfur in its physical essence, as well as the spirit of the sulfur, so that it does not fall to dust. The salt compresses the powers of the anguish, and this compressed life is the "mercurial" life. This is the life of the anguish—that is, of the sulfur—and it separates the <term>matter</term> <note>original: "Materia."</note> according to the forms of nature. It also separates the matter of the free delight into two essences—first into a watery and an oily essence, and then into a physical essence.

17. The physical essence is twofold, corresponding to both the darkness and the light. According to the property of the harsh desire, it creates a sandy or stony nature within the watery property; this is the origin of stones. Understand this to come out of the sulfurous property—that is, out of the sulfur's water.

18. The other property, regarding the <term>mortification</term> <note>original: "mortification." In alchemy, the process of breaking down or "killing" a substance to release its inner spirit.</note> in the <term>Salnitral Flagrat</term> <note>original: "Salnitral Flagrat." A term Boehme uses for the sudden, explosive flash of life or consciousness, like the ignition of saltpeter.</note>, is common running water. The other corporeal water is the metallic body, arising from the property of the <term>free delight</term> <note>original: "free Lubet." The divine spontaneous will or joy.</note> within the manifested form. <margin>Or, Out of.</margin> From this watery property (where the sulfur is in the water), it produces trees, herbs, and everything that grows in the earthly property—that is, in the mortified or dead substantiality, which nevertheless possesses a <margin>Dumb.</margin> senseless life, specifically a vegetative one.

19. The oily property is also twofold, according to how it is impressed into matter. One part forces its way back toward freedom, seeking to be free from the wrath of the compression; this is the good spirit, the light within the oil. The other part yields itself to the <term>anguish of the sulfur</term> <note>original: "Anguish of the Brimstone." The tension or "squeeze" of physical existence.</note> and remains within the physical body. It unites and adapts itself to each thing according to its "salt-property." For example, in a fiery salt, the oil is fiery; in a bitter salt, it is bitter; and in an astringent salt, it is astringent, and so on.

20. The first property, according to the light, is sweet in all things. The other property of the oil depends on the form—that is, the taste of the thing, whether it be sweet, sour, astringent, sharp, or bitter. This can be seen and known in herbs: in some, it is a bitter poison, while in others, it is a healing for that same poison. However, if the poisonous property is broken by <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercury." Here representing the active, mediating spirit or life-force.</note> in the "oil of meekness," then the love of the light also inclines itself into the oil. This is because the origin of both properties comes from one single will, though it is altered during the compression. This is similar to how the Devil, when he was an angel, changed himself into a poisonous, devilish property, and how Adam changed from a heavenly property into an earthly one.

21. Whatever grows, lives, and moves in this world consists of <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: "Sulphur." One of the three primary alchemical principles, representing the soul and the combustible quality.</note>. Mercury is the life within that sulfur, and salt is the physical being created by Mercury’s "hunger"—even though bodies take many forms. Whatever the property of the sulfur and salt may be, the "ingrafted oil" follows that same property as it springs up through its power, for the oil provides the inner virtue or influence in everything. Within this physical or "impressed" oil, there is another oil: the spiritual one that gives us light. This spiritual oil belongs to a different <term>Principle</term> <note>original: "Principle." In Boehme’s cosmology, a distinct realm of reality (e.g., the dark world, the light world, or the physical world).</note>. it receives no other influence into itself except the delight of love; it is divine essentiality. Therefore, God’s own essence is near to all things, but not essentially *in* all things. It belongs to another principle, yet it inclines itself toward all things. So far as a thing has any of the divine property within it, it receives power from the divine, whether it is a plant or an animal.

22. All sharpness of taste is salt, whatever it may be in this world, without exception. All smell proceeds from sulfur <note>original: "Brimstone." In Boehme's alchemy, sulfur represents the combustible, energetic principle of matter.</note>, and Mercury is the "distinguisher" in all motion (or feeling), whether in smell, power, or taste. But by my use of the term "Mercury," I mean the sphere of the birth of all essences, as mentioned before; not a dead mercury <note>Boehme is referring to the spiritual principle of Mercury—movement and communication—rather than the liquid metal found in a lab.</note>, but a living one—the strongest kind, according to the property of the "dry poison," etc.

<margin>If he can only get.</margin>
23. Now it is necessary for the artist and physician to know these things; otherwise, he cannot cure any sickness or disease unless he hits upon the cure by chance. He must know how the oil in the body has been poisoned and what kind of "hunger" Mercury has during the sickness—what it is longing for. For if the physician can obtain the salt that matches the property of Mercury's hunger (the thing it desires) along with the kind of oil it wishes to have, then the sickness is over very quickly. This is because Mercury turns its oil back into the property of the love of the light, whereupon the life begins to shine brightly again.

24. For every disease in the body is nothing other than a corruption or poisoning of the oil from which the light of life burns or shines. When the light of life shines or burns clearly in the oil, it expels and drives away all poisonous influences and operations, just as the day expels the night.

<margin>Sting.</margin>
25. For if the oil from which life burns is infected (or inflamed) with a poisonous Mercury or salt—whether this comes from the stars <note>original: "the Constellation." Early modern medicine often linked physical health to astrological influences.</note> or from the salt in food (meaning from a contrary source)—a loathing (or nauseous disgust) arises in the oil. The oil always seeks to vomit this out, and Mercury assists in this. Then Mercury works eagerly and disturbs itself more and more within the sulfurous fire, continually laboring to drive out the <term>Abominate</term> <note>original: "Abominate." A term for an impurity or offensive substance that the body finds "abominable" and tries to reject.</note>. However, in this harsh effort, Mercury only inflames itself and further kindles its own inward form. Consequently, the oil grows more dark and poisonous until, at last, the oil becomes entirely watery and earthy. Then the light, and also the fire, goes out, and Mercury—along with the sulfurous spirit—departs from it, just as when a candle is extinguished. Thus, Mercury passes out with the sulfurous spirit in death's baneful steam <margin>sting</margin>, until it also is famished. For a time, it may sustain itself in the <term>sidereal body</term> <note>original: "Syderial Body." The "star-body" or astral body that was thought to survive for a short time after physical death.</note> which travels with it; but when Mercury has consumed and starved its property within the spirit of the Great World <note>The "Great World" or Macrocosm; the universe as a whole.</note>, then the temporal life is entirely gone.

25. For as soon as the light of the "Vital Oil" is extinguished, the physical body decays into putrefaction—that is, back into the *Fiat* <note>original: "Fiat". However, this cannot happen unless there was a good quality of oil within it—namely, from the divine "Essentiality." Only in this quality, which is capable of receiving the divine essence, can the light rekindle itself again.

26. For the divine Essentiality, or this heavenly Mercury, changes the dead oil back into its own essence and becomes its life. The outward Mercury, which ruled the physical life, does not return; it was only a temporary mirror of the eternal. Instead, it is changed into another state (or "source"). Once suffocated, it passes back into the "Mystery" <note>The "Mysterium Magnum," or Great Mystery, which Boehme describes as the chaos or potentiality from which all things are created.</note> from which it first emerged during the creation of the world, and the body also enters that same Mystery.

27. Thus it remains until another movement of the Deity—namely, a "Separation," where the evil (which contained death) shall be separated from the good. Then the *Verbum Fiat* <note>original: "Verbum Fiat". Latin for "The Word: Let it be done."</note> shall restore and bring forth what fell into it through death.

28. But Mercury contains another property: an oil from the light, which makes it so strong and potent and serves as its food and preservation. If this oil can be separated from it, it becomes a healing "tincture" and a powerful enkindling of all "obscured lives"—that is, of all diseases and illnesses. For the joyful life lies within this oil, and it is a "hunger" for life, seeking to rekindle the weak and lift it up.

## CHAP. VII.

-> *How Adam in Paradise, and Lucifer, were beautiful angels, and how they were corrupted and ruined through imagination and pride.* <-

-> *The Process.* <-

1. We will provide an opportunity for consideration to the earnest researcher and seeker; if he understands our meaning, he shall indeed be able to find the noble Philosopher’s Stone—but only if he is chosen for it by God and his life also stands in the heavenly *Mercury*. Otherwise, we are a *mystery* to him, and we will represent it to him in likenesses <note>original: "Similitudes"</note>, in the most clear and yet *mystical* manner.

2. When *Adam was created in Paradise*, the heavenly *Mercury* led him then; his life burned in a pure oil, and therefore his eyes were heavenly. An alchemical term referring to the "Cagaster," or the corrupt, diseased, and mortal substance of the fallen world.</note>. This means the wateriness in the mortal property was manifest in his oil and penetrated it, so that the *Mercury* in him became an anxious poison, which previously in his oil was an exaltation of joyfulness.

10. He is like wood that is burnt to a coal, which only glows and no longer has any true light in it, nor any oil or water; that is how it went with him. Now, in his own property—namely, in his life-forms—nothing springs forth but a stinging, envious property, where one form hates and annoys the other, and yet they continue to beget each other.

11. And the Serpent was likewise formed this way, though not by its own aspiring pride. Rather, when God said, "Let all sorts of beasts come forth, each according to his property (or kind)," then beasts came forth out of every property of Nature as it was revealed in the separation <note>original: "Se-Veration"</note> when God moved Himself toward the Creation. 

The Devil wished to dominate the love and meekness of God, <margin>Or, set his desire upon the anger.</margin> and he put his desire also into the "Anger"—that is, into the austere power where the poisonous life arises—namely, into the **Fiat** <note>original: "Fiat". Latin for "let it be done," referring to God’s creative command.</note> of the wrathful property. From this form proceeded vipers, serpents, toads, and other venomous worms. It is not that the Devil made them—he cannot do that—but as the desire was within the impression of the **Fiat**, so the creature became, in both evil and good.
